recall_moments.answer: Quadrant 3, because it is urgent to them but not important to your goals.
recall_moments.tempting_wrong: Quadrant 1, because it feels like you must do it right away.
recall_moments.question: Where does a colleague's quick favor belong?

strategy.rationale: Shows the framework in action with a running example of a daily workload, allowing practitioners to map it to their own roles.
strategy.signature_move: Demonstrate categorising a task, then fade support until the learner handles a new task independently.
strategy.name: worked_example_led

audience.motivation: Wants a reliable method to handle overflowing inboxes without working late.
audience.context: Corporate office environments where constant requests from colleagues interrupt core projects.
audience.assumed_prior: Basic workplace norms and the experience of having too much to do
audience.why: Improving productivity and reducing daily stress

title: Workplace Essentials: Time Management

mayer.contiguity: text and graphics aligned in sec_quadrants
mayer.pre_training: sec_distinction defines terms before the framework

arcs.relevance: mapped directly to a busy employee's inbox

misconceptions.why_tempting: They require immediate action and often relate to other people's priorities, creating psychological pressure.
misconceptions.belief: Urgent tasks with short deadlines are always the most important ones to do first.

practice_ladder.description: The narrator completely sorts a sample inbox into the four quadrants.
A colleague asks for a quick favor, and the viewer predicts the quadrant.
The viewer must draft the polite reply declining the task to protect a core priority.

transfer_tasks: The next time you plan tomorrow's workload, identify your single most important task and block it on your calendar before checking emails.
performance: Prioritises daily tasks using the Eisenhower framework to reduce end-of-day rush.

arc.bridge_from_prior: Connects the familiar feeling of being busy but unproductive to the need for distinguishing urgent from important tasks.
arc.promise: You will learn a reliable method to separate true priorities from mere distractions.
arc.payoff: Returns to the opening scenario, showing the employee leaving on time with their critical project complete and tomorrow scheduled.

sections.goal: the viewer can define urgent and important tasks
sections.carrier: A split screen comparing a ringing phone with a long-term goal document, shifting focus between them
A 2x2 grid drawing on screen with task cards visually sliding into each appropriate box
sections.goal: the viewer can classify tasks into the four quadrants of the Eisenhower framework

sections.carrier: An inbox message appearing on screen, replaced by a typed reply that politely declines the request
sections.goal: the viewer can follow the framework to decline a low-priority task

sections.carrier: A calendar view populating with blocked out time slots for priority projects
sections.goal: the viewer can schedule important tasks before urgent demands arrive

hook.sketch: Imagine logging off late, exhausted by urgent emails, yet your core project is untouched. You stare at tomorrow's overflowing inbox, dreading the same cycle again.
